name: L-serine
short: ALS trial, 20 people: 3 died (a report: about the number expected), 2 withdrew with gut problems. Hereditary neuropathy, 18 adults: no serious related effects. 1 of 24 children stopped (irritability).
text: Human safety data come from small trials of L-serine in neurological diseases, taken by mouth in the ALS and neuropathy trials (the children's trial abstract does not state the route). In a 6-month phase I trial in 20 patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) at four dose levels, one withdrew before treatment, two withdrew with gastrointestinal problems and three died during the trial, which a later report of a phase I trial of oral L-serine in 20 patients with ALS called about the expected number (neither abstract says whether the two reports describe the same trial); disease progression was compared with historical placebo controls rather than a concurrent placebo group, and the authors concluded that L-serine was generally well tolerated and did not appear to accelerate functional decline. In a 1-year randomised placebo-controlled trial in 18 adults with hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1, there were no serious adverse effects related to L-serine. In a 52-week non-randomised, open-label, single-arm trial in 24 children aged 2 to 18 with GRIN-related encephalopathy, one patient stopped treatment because of irritability and insomnia. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
